text: Every shadow has an owner.
This one was going home.
Previously, on the Keeper’s Island.
A man who never aged came to collect four ships. Gus’s mother burned his contract in the cave, and the sea took Silas Crane.
But his shadow stayed behind, on the wall. Smiling.
Monday. The quay was busy for the first time since the storm. Parcels, nets, gossip.
Gus counted people out of habit. Seven. Then he counted shadows.
Eight. The eighth had nobody standing over it.
It stood on its own at the empty berth where the barge had been. Upright. Wearing a bowler hat.
Nobody else on the quay saw it. Or nobody else would say.
When Gus looked again, the berth was empty, and the noon sun shone straight through where it had stood.
The post office smelled of candle wax and other people’s letters. Wren was waiting, as if she had heard.
The man who sold his shadow sold it to a buyer in a pale suit. Your Mr Crane.
And a shadow without its master does one thing, Gus. It goes home. To the family that sold it.
Gus asked her the man’s name.
Wren blew out the candle instead. Some names, she said, you only say in daylight.
At midnight the window of the post office went dark. Then the harbour office. Then the lamp by the jetty.
Not blown out. Swallowed. As if something had walked past each one and taken the light with it.
From the cottage step, Gus watched the dark come up the cliff path. Lamp by lamp. Toward him.
Mabel’s tail went thick as a rope.
Then his own flame leaned away from the path, the way a candle leans from a cold door.
Just beyond the light, something was standing. Waiting for it to go out.
Marlo had watched the lights die from the jetty, and run the whole cliff path with every lantern off the ferry.
Twelve lanterns, in a ring around the cottage, an arm’s length apart.
At the edge of the ring, the dark stopped. It pressed against the light, the way the sea presses against a wall.
And in the dark, something smiled.
It could not come in. Not while the lanterns burned.
Marlo checked the oil. She did not say how much was left. She did not have to.
The next night Gus kept the lamp himself, on the step below it, with the ring of lanterns still burning in his eyes.
A shadow that walks. A shadow that cannot cross light. A shadow that goes home to the family that sold it.
And a family name Wren would only say in daylight.
The lanterns held until a quarter to four. Then the dark went back into the rock, as if it had somewhere to be.
At noon, Wren opened the wreckers’ ledger at the very last page.
Nineteen twenty-six. Sold, one shadow, to S. Crane, for four years of life at sea.
Signed by the last of the wreckers. Your grandfather, Gus.
Gus had his grandfather’s watch. His grandfather’s cap. His grandfather’s name.
He had never once asked what his grandfather had been.
Now his grandfather’s shadow had come home, looking for family.
Dunn had heard the name from Wren before Gus reached the quay. He was waiting with a small black diary.
My father wrote it down. Your grandfather walked off his sunk boat without a mark on him. And without a shadow.
Four years later, to the day, he walked back into the sea. My father said he was smiling.
Four years. The price his mother paid. The smile on the cave wall.
It had never been Crane’s shadow at all. Crane had only been wearing it.
Pause here. The shadow came home to the family that sold it.
Gus’s grandfather sold it in 1926. His grandfather is gone. His mother has her own shadow back.
Thursday, low tide. Marlo rowed them in through the crack, oars shipped, the cave glowing green around them.
On the wall where the smile had been, there was only wet rock.
Rollo found the only thing it had left behind.
A dent in the sand, the shape of a bowler hat. And a long dark stain, as if something had been dragged toward the water.
Toward the deep pool at the back of the cave. The one Mabel will not go near.
Gus knelt at the pool with his lantern. Under the surface, something darker than the water turned over.
Then a hand made of nothing but shadow closed around the light, and pulled.
Gus went with it. Knees, then hands, then the cold.
And Mabel, who sits down very fast for fish and fear, did neither. She jumped.
She came up with her teeth in his collar and the lantern still lit, and hauled until Marlo could grab them both.
But the flame it had touched had gone thin and pale, like a lamp seen through ice.
Pip had a theory. Gulls usually do. At noon he would count every person on the island, and every shadow.
Two hundred and six people. Two hundred and seven shadows.
He found the extra one on the cliff path. It was walking beside Gus, step for step, close enough to hold his hand.
Gus had two shadows now. One of them wore a hat.
Pip told Gus. Gus did not turn around.
He said he had felt it since the pool. Cold, on his left side, like standing too close to the sea.
Gus had not seen his mother since the ferry came home. At midnight she was at the end of the jetty, facing the sea.
Her shadow lay on the boards beside her, small and ordinary. She seemed to be keeping an eye on it.
It wants a keeper, Gus. It belonged to one once. It will take yours, and your light with it.
A shadow must fall away from its light. Give it nowhere to fall.
Then she stepped off the end of the jetty, and the sea closed over her like a door.
Gus stood there while the lamp came round three times. Nowhere to fall.
That night Gus slept with his lantern lit, for the first time since he was a boy.
Mabel slept on his chest. She had not left his side since the pool, and she was not about to start.
Saturday at dusk, they worked it out on the back of a ferry timetable.
Every light throws a shadow on its far side. Light something from every side at once, and there is no far side left.
The tower above. The under-lamp below. Twelve lanterns in a ring. Wren’s candle, Dunn’s harbour lamp, Marlo’s ferry lights.
And Gus’s lantern in the middle. As bait.
Wren asked who would stand in the middle when the dark came for its keeper.
Gus said that was the job. It always had been.
One last pause. A shadow always falls away from its light.
The tower above. The cave lamp below. A ring of lanterns all round. And Gus in the middle.
At three o’clock the island looked like a birthday cake. Every window, every lantern, the tower, the ferry, all burning at once.
At the foot of the tower, Gus stood alone in the ring, and waited.
At three twelve, the dark came up out of the door in the rock and crossed the grass toward him.
It reached the first lantern, and its edge went thin as paper.
Light from the tower. Light from below. Light from every side.
The shadow turned, and turned, looking for somewhere to fall. There was nowhere left.
In the middle of all that light, the bowler hat came apart like smoke.
What was left wore a flat cap with a peak. A keeper’s cap. The one hanging by Gus’s door.
Gus said the only word he could think of.
Grandad.
The shadow knelt, the way a tired man kneels, and the smile went out of it.
Then it slid down the steps, under the door in the rock, and away toward the sea. Not hunting. Going home.
At four the lanterns burned out one by one, and there was nothing left in the dark to wait for them.
Sunday at dawn, Gus walked out to the north rocks. She was there, the way he knew she would be.
Two people. Two shadows. He counted twice.
Your grandfather sold his shadow to Crane. Crane must have sold his own to someone, long before.
A man does not live a hundred years on one shadow, Gus.
That morning Dunn found Crane’s grey barge drifting empty outside the harbour, and towed it in.
In the wheelhouse, the ledger lay open at a new page. One line, in a thin sloping hand, the ink still wet.
The Keeper’s Island. Payable to the bearer.
